headlines.title: Stocks making the biggest moves premarket: Alphabet, Caterpillar, Eli Lilly, DoorDash & more
headlines.summary: These are the stocks posting the largest moves in the premarket.
headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves premarket: GOOGL, CAT, LLY, DASH Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Check out the companies making the biggest moves in premarket trading: Alphabet — The Google parent dropped 11% after its third-quarter earnings showed the company posted negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion. Its core search revenue of $63.35 billion missed the $64.96 billion estimate from analysts. Total company revenue of $127.58 billion also missed LSEG expectations of $128.22 billion. Caterpillar — Shares slid 9% even after the company reported third-quarter earnings and revenue that beat the Street. The company earned an adjusted $7.20 per share on revenue of $20.68 billion. Analysts polled by LSEG expected a profit of $7.08 per share on revenue of $20.55 billion. However, sales for its construction industries business came in slightly below estimates. DoorDash , Maplebear — DoorDash announced it is acquiring the Instacart parent for $65 per share. That is an 11% premium from Maplebear's closing price on Wednesday. DoorDash also reported a revenue and EBITDA beat for its third quarter. Maplebear was up 4.8% before trading was halted, while DoorDash rose 7%. Eli Lilly — The Zepbound and Mounjaro maker handily beat expectations for its third quarter, sending shares 4% higher. Eli Lilly saw adjusted earnings of $7.48 per share, compared with the consensus estimate $6.26 a share, per LSEG. Revenue came in at $24.4 billion, topping the $22.61 billion expected from analysts. Marvell Technology , Lumentum — Lumentum shares jumped 5% after Bloomberg News reported, citing sources that the data center optics manufacturer was in talks to be acquired by Marvell. A deal could be announced as soon as next week, the report said . Marvell shares dropped more than 11%. Microsoft — The software giant rose 2% after the company reported a beat on the top and bottom lines for its fiscal first-quarter earnings. Revenue came in at $92.28 billion, ahead of the $90.69 billion expected by LSEG. Meanwhile, adjusted earnings of $4.89 per share was better than the $4.73 expected by analysts. Revenue in the mega-cap's key Azure cloud business grew 48% year over year. Shell — The oil major climbed 3.6% after it nearly doubled its third-quarter profit from the year prior to $10.81 billion. Analysts polled by LSEG were expecting $9.92 billion. Norwegian Cruise Line — The cruise operator jumped 9.5% following its beat on the top and bottom lines. Norwegian reported adjusted earnings of $1.12 per share, topping the consensus estimate of 93 cents, according to FactSet. Revenue was $2.95 billion, versus the $2.88 billion anticipated by analysts. Chipotle Mexican Grill — Shares gained nearly 8% after the burrito chain reported same-store sales that beat estimates. Same-store sales in the third quarter grew 2.1%, versus the 1.5% increase analysts polled by FactSet anticipated. ServiceNow — The enterprise software company tumbled 20%. Third-quarter adjusted profit of $1 per share missed the LSEG consensus expectation of $1.02 a share. Subscription revenue guidance for the fourth quarter ranged from $4.245 billion to $4.255 billion, while the FactSet consensus called for $4.25 billion. Fortinet — The cybersecurity company plummeted 25.5%. Non-GAAP gross margin for the third quarter came in at 79.6%, while analysts polled by LSEG sought 80.1%. Separately, top and bottom-line results beat the Street's expectations. Sprouts Farmers Market — The Phoenix-based grocery chain plunged 23% after third-quarter earnings per share, revenue and same-store sales all trailed analysts' consensus estimates, according to FactSet data. Harley-Davidson — Shares of the motorcycle maker dropped 5% following a revenue miss in its latest quarter. Harley-Davidson posted revenue of $964.0 million, falling short of the StreetAccount consensus estimate of $1.07 billion. On the other hand, adjusted EBITDA of $93.9 million topped the FactSet consensus of $78.9 million. Crocs — The footwear stock surged nearly 18% after Crocs posted third-quarter earnings that beat expectations, and issued stronger-than-expected current quarter guidance. It posted earnings of $3.69 per share, excluding items, on revenue of $1.04 billion. Analysts polled by FactSet anticipated earnings of $3.31 per share on revenue of $1.00 billion. eBay — Shares climbed more than 6% after the company reported stronger-than-expected third-quarter results. Revenue rose 14% to $3.2 billion, while gross merchandise volume increased 15%. Growth from Depop, accelerating GMV, and raised full-year guidance gave investors further confidence in eBay's strategy. Honeywell Aerospace — The aerospace company was down 4% even after raising its full-year outlook for pro forma standalone adjusted earnings per share, calling for $7.85 to $8. The company also announced an initial quarterly cash dividend of 40 cents per share. Carvana — The used car dealer climbed 8%. Carvana third-quarter revenue and adjusted EBITDA topped the numbers Wall Street had been expecting, and it said the Securities and Exchange Commission closed a previously disclosed investigation and would not take any enforcement action. CNBC's Darla Mercado, Fred Imbert, Sarah Min, Paulina Likos, Scott Schnipper, Deena Zaidi and Nick Wells contributed reporting.

headlines.article_text: DoorDash to acquire Instacart for $17 billion Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points DoorDash will acquire Instacart for $17 billion, the companies announced Thursday. The deal unites two delivery giants under one roof, with DoorDash's focus on restaurants and Instacart's robust stable of grocery partners. Speculation about a deal has swirled since last week. In this article DASH CART Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 0:50 00:50 DoorDash to acquire Instacart for $65/share in cash & stock Squawk Box DoorDash will acquire Instacart for about $17 billion, the companies announced Thursday, uniting two delivery giants under one roof. DoorDash will pay $65 a share in cash and stock, an 11% premium to Instacart's closing price on Wednesday, and about 26% above Instacart's closing price on Oct. 22, the last trading day before reports surfaced of a possible sale. Shares of DoorDash jumped more than 8% in premarket trading following news of the deal, while Instacart traded near the flatline. The deal is slated to close at the end of 2027 or early 2028, the companies said. DoorDash expects to retain Instacart's brand, enterprise technology products and app once the deal closes. DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said in a statement that grocery is "one of the hardest things to get right online." He pointed to difficulties around picking the right inventory and delivering perishable goods to customers' doorsteps without damaging them on the way. "Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day," Xu said. "Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery." Read more CNBC tech news Amazon’s anti-tokenmaxxing memo says engineers should be pickier about using AI Chart: Anthropic’s cash pile towers over nearly every U.S. company Google alters its cloud playbook, enlisting partners to sell more AI chips A guide to some of the biggest risks in Anthropic's IPO prospectus DoorDash reported its third-quarter results alongside the deal announcement. Adjusted earnings per share were $1.06, beating the average analyst estimate of 84 cents per share, according to LSEG. Revenue came in at $4.62 billion, topping LSEG estimates of $4.56 billion. Marketplace gross order value, which tracks the total dollar value of orders on its platform, grew 36% year over year to $33.9 billion, beating consensus estimates of $33.6 billion. Total orders reached 993 million, up 28% from a year ago. Speculation of a deal has swirled since last week, when The Information reported Instacart was exploring a sale and had held talks with companies including Uber and DoorDash. On Monday, several outlets reported DoorDash was in advanced discussions to acquire Instacart and that the deal could value Instacart at about $17 billion. Sources familiar with the matter had told CNBC on Wednesday that the deal could be announced as soon as Thursday morning. Acquiring Instacart would give DoorDash a bigger presence in online grocery delivery. DoorDash got its start in food delivery, and since then, it has added more retailers to its marketplace, such as Sephora, Macy's , Staples and Anthropologie. It's recently made grocery a bigger priority, adding a stable of regional grocers after announcing a partnership with Kroger last year. Instacart , which went public in 2023, was one of the biggest beneficiaries of a pandemic-driven surge in grocery delivery services, but it has struggled to maintain that momentum. In December Instacart agreed to pay $60 million to settle allegations by the Federal Trade Commission that it misled users with false advertising and deployed "unlawful subscription enrollment" practices. Instacart (Maplebear) and Doordash stock chart. The service has also faced increasingly stiff competition from companies like Amazon and Walmart . After slowing its brick-and-mortar grocery effort, Amazon has doubled down on its online grocery business and leveraged its vast fulfillment footprint to speed up deliveries of household essentials, pantry staples and perishables. Both Amazon and Walmart have pushed further into same- and next-day delivery, which poses a threat to Instacart and DoorDash's on-demand delivery model. Analysts have noted that a potential combination of Instacart and DoorDash could attract antitrust scrutiny given the companies' market overlap. Third-party delivery platforms "remain a minority of total grocery consumption, but slicing and dicing the online market more narrowly or from a perspective of the grocers as enterprise customers can make approvals more challenging," Wedbush analysts wrote in a Monday research note. -- CNBC's MacKenzie Sigalos contributed to this report. watch now VIDEO 1:02 01:02 DoorDash deal to buy Instacart to be announced as early as Thursday morning Closing Bell: Overtime Choose CNBC as your preferred source on Google and never miss a moment from the most trusted name in business news.

headlines.title: AI build-out hits snag as Google and Microsoft put off raising capex forecasts
headlines.summary: Microsoft and Alphabet both reported capital expenditures that fell short of estimates, adding to concern over the cost of the AI build-out.
headlines.article_text: AI buildout hits snag as Google and Microsoft hold capex forecasts Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Microsoft and Google both reported capital expenditures that fell short of analysts' estimates. Amy Hood, Microsoft's CFO, said on the company's earnings call that third-party providers of AI chips had delays that will push out some available capacity until the first half of 2027. The disclosures added to investor concerns about neoclouds, which are seeing their cost of capital rise as fears mount about their debt loads. In this article GOOGL MSFT Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Sundar Pichai, CEO, Google and Satya Nadella, CEO of Microsoft. Denis Balibouse | Ruben Sprich | Reuters The past few quarters of hyperscaler earnings have been marked by ever-increasing capital expenditure forecasts as tech giants race to build out artificial intelligence infrastructure to meet what they describe as insatiable demand. At least for the moment, Microsoft and Alphabet are telling a slightly different story. In their earnings reports Wednesday, both companies shared capex figures that came up shy of analysts' estimates. Microsoft reduced its capex forecast for the year to $170 billion from $175 billion, and Alphabet held its guidance at $195 billion to $205 billion. The numbers suggest a slowdown is nowhere in sight, but they do represent another potential point of concern for the AI build-out. Shares of neoclouds CoreWeave , Nebius and IREN all dropped after the reports, as did Oracle , which is one of the biggest spenders on AI infrastructure. Microsoft CFO Amy Hood said on the software company's earnings call that third-party providers of graphics processing units had delays that will push out some available capacity until the first half of 2027. She didn't provide names, but Microsoft relies on CoreWeave, IREN and Nebius, among others. Anat Ashkenazi , Alphabet's finance chief, told analysts that outside computing power "came online only at the very end of Q3." Alphabet shares tumbled about 10% in extended trading as the company missed on earnings and revenue and reported negative free cash flow of more than $9 billion. Plenty of Alphabet shareholders remain faithful. "We are pleased with what we see and what we heard, and trust management's approach to their AI spending," Chris Ballard, managing director of Check Capital Management, wrote in an email to CNBC. Investors will get a final read on hyperscaler capex for the quarter when Amazon reports results after the close Thursday. In Meta's earnings report last week, the company said it expects full-year capex of $135 billion to $145 billion, raising the bottom of the range from $130 billion. Like with Alphabet, Meta shares sank as the company reported negative free cash flow. watch now VIDEO 4:33 04:33 Free cashflow or AI capex? Markets don't know what they want, says Albion's Ware Squawk Box Asia Delays from emerging neocloud partners have occurred before at Microsoft, but they're more critical now as Anthropic gets set to go public. Anthropic counts on infrastructure from Amazon, Google and Microsoft for much of its computing needs, alongside capacity from SpaceX , Lambda and Nscale, which filed to go public in September but hasn't updated its prospectus in weeks. At times this year, Anthropic's Claude assistant has been unavailable due to climbing demand. Rival OpenAI , which has said an initial public offering in 2027 is likely, is also in constant need of more capacity. One big challenge for the market is that the neoclouds require billions of dollars in outside capital to fuel their build-outs but don't have investment-grade credit ratings. With interest rates rising and concerns about their debt loads mounting, lenders are pulling out of the market. Last week, analysts at Gartner shared with CNBC the firm's prediction that, by 2030, 80% of neocloud companies will either be absorbed or completely cease operations. Nvidia -backed neocloud Firmus, based in Australia, withdrew plans to go public earlier this month, despite boasting large usage commitments from Meta and OpenAI. None of that is to suggest the AI build-out is over, or even close to plateauing. Microsoft's Hood said Wednesday that she sees capital spending accelerating in the first half of 2027 thanks to higher component costs and the delayed deliveries. As a group, hyperscaler capex is expected to top $1 trillion next year and, according to some estimates , continue rising from there. Despite the third-quarter capex shortfall, investors cheered Microsoft's report on Wednesday as the company beat earnings and revenue estimates, driven by 48% sales growth in its Azure cloud business. "We view the quarter as further validation of Microsoft's AI-led growth opportunity," Cantor analysts led by Thomas Blakey wrote in a Wednesday note to clients. They recommend buying Microsoft stock, and they pushed up their one-year price target to $630 from $608. headlines.title: Alphabet earnings miss reflects first real sign that AI is taking a bite out of search
headlines.summary: Wall Street hammered Alphabet for an earnings miss that included weaker-than-expected revenue out of the company's core business.
headlines.article_text: Alphabet earnings miss first sign AI is taking a bite out of search Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Wall Street hammered Alphabet for an earnings miss that included weaker-than-expected revenue in the company's core business. Revenue in the search and other segment grew 12% from a year ago to roughly $63 billion, but came in below estimates for the second straight quarter. Regarding new AI agents and bots, Deepwater Asset Management's Gene Munster said, "These things are going to be a force." In this article GOOGL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Sundar Pichai, CEO of Alphabet, during the Google I/O Developers Conference in Mountain View, California, May 19, 2026. David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Images In Alphabet's across-the-board earnings miss , one segment stood out above all else: search. Revenue in the search and other segment grew 12% from a year ago to roughly $63 billion, but came in below estimates for the second straight quarter. At the same time, Google said search query growth on the platform was the strongest it's been in five years. The gap between usage and revenue within the search giant's flagship business is becoming harder to dismiss as more people turn to artificial intelligence bots and agents, including tools offered by Google. Since the early days of ChatGPT, analysts have predicted that traditional search will get eclipsed by AI, and warned that Google will have to figure out new ways to make money. While search remains a massive business, early signs of a shift are appearing. "These things are going to be a force," Deepwater Asset Management's Gene Munster told CNBC's " Fast Money " after the earnings report, referring to new AI-powered services. Munster said that if "personalized bots" take off, "that will become for a lot of people the starting point of commerce, which impacts where Google is." watch now VIDEO 5:16 05:16 AI search queries hurt Alphabet's core business, says Deepwater's Gene Munster Fast Money Alphabet executives said foreign exchange was the biggest factor behind the deceleration in search revenue in the period, and said the currency impact would be even greater in the fourth quarter. The stock plummeted about 10% in extended trading, reflecting the weaker-than-expected earnings report and negative free cash flow of $9 billion for the quarter, three times the estimated deficit. In the second quarter, Alphabet's free cash flow went negative for the first time in its history as a public company, at $5.9 billion. Google has spent much of the past year telling investors that it needs to pour money into AI infrastructure and services to meet unending demand from consumers and businesses. Google's Gemini model has allowed the company to stay competitive with Anthropic and OpenAI , and its Gemini-powered enterprise services have proven to be a hit with customers. The company also says that Gemini is strengthening its core digital ads business, as it uses AI to improve its ability to understand user intent and make advertising more relevant. “We continue to accelerate the deployment of Gemini models across our entire ads infrastructure to boost performance,” Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler said on the earnings call. Read more CNBC tech news Amazon’s anti-tokenmaxxing memo says engineers should be pickier about using AI Chart: Anthropic’s cash pile towers over nearly every U.S. company Google alters its cloud playbook, enlisting partners to sell more AI chips A guide to some of the biggest risks in Anthropic's IPO prospectus The company made what Schindler called its “biggest update to product listing ads in a decade” during the third quarter, adding new AI capabilities. “Overall, AI is accelerating our ads development and drives the majority of our product launches,” Schindler said. Advertisers are also rapidly adopting AI tools. In the third quarter, Gemini models helped advertisers generate more than 1.5 billion campaign assets, up more than sevenfold from a year earlier, Schindler said. But none of that addresses revenue growth for search, which slid from 19% in the first quarter to 17% in the second, before falling to 12% in the third. Analysts at UBS wrote in a note that the results are "going to bring Search cannibalization fears right back to the forefront." And Mizuho analyst Jordan Klein said the numbers are an issue for search and YouTube. "This elevates the fear around AI and agentic taking share from Search and YT and hurting their AI monetization narrative," Klein wrote in a note after the earnings report. Cloud gives Alphabet its AI payoff Where Alphabet's AI bet is very much paying off is in its cloud business. Revenue in that division, which is racing to catch up to Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure, more than doubled in the quarter to nearly $31 billion. Cloud backlog also reached roughly $560 billion, reflecting enormous contracted demand for AI infrastructure. Management said it expects just more than half of that backlog to be recognized over the next 24 months. In Microsoft's quarterly earnings report , which also landed after the bell Wednesday, the software maker said Azure revenue increased 48% from a year earlier to $33.2 billion. Cloud demand is a big reason for Alphabet to keep spending. The company maintained its full-year 2026 capital expenditure forecast of $195 billion to $205 billion and said spending will increase significantly in 2027. Some of that is for its tensor processing units , or TPUs, which compete with Nvidia's graphics processing units. Alphabet just started selling them to outside customers in the second quarter. Google released its 7th generation TPU, Ironwood, in November 2025, a decade after making its first custom ASIC for AI in 2015. Google Customer agreements first show up in Google Cloud’s backlog, and the company has to spend money building the systems before it can deliver them and recognize the associated revenue. “You see cash going out and we’re building up the inventory base,” Alphabet CFO Anat Ashkenazi said on the earnings call. “As we start delivering and billing customers for these TPU systems, then you see cash coming in.” Still, Google has to contend with concerns about its longtime cash cow. Gil Luria, an analyst at D.A. Davidson, said the fears that existed from 2023 to 2025 about the AI effect appear to finally be showing up in Google's business. "Investors will now worry that the miss in Search, YouTube and Subscription, leading to a profit miss, are an indication that AI has finally come for Google," Luria wrote in an email. "We would not rush to conclusions based on one quarter, but will definitely need to reassess what the world of agentic commerce means for Google."
